profile.behavior: Active foliage gleaner that forages especially among outer treetop branches, probing and picking insects, hovering at foliage, and sallying for flying prey. It also takes nectar, sap, and fruit, migrates mainly at night, and is territorial during the breeding season.
field_marks: Small, delicate warbler with a short tail
Slender, dark, slightly downcurved bill and dark eye
Yellow underparts marked with narrow dark “tiger” streaks
Adult male has a chestnut cheek framed by yellow; females and immatures are duller with a grayish cheek
Olive upperparts and dark wings with a conspicuous white patch or wingbars
Dark, slender legs and white undertail coverts
profile.habitat: Breeds in mature boreal forests dominated by spruce and balsam fir, often near openings or forest edges. During migration it uses varied woodland, scrub, and thickets; nonbreeding habitats include shrubby plantings, second growth, pine and broadleaf forest, dry forest, and mangroves.

findings: The primary specimen is a convincing adult male Cape May Warbler: yellow underparts with fine dark streaking, a chestnut auricular patch framed by yellow, olive upperparts, dark wings with a conspicuous white patch, white undertail coverts, and a short tail agree with the reference photographs and direct identification sources.

The proportions are credible for a small, delicate, short-tailed warbler. The dark bill is slender and only subtly downcurved, consistent with the clearest side-profile references; neither depicted head has a truncated, reversed, or materially exaggerated mandible.

The primary specimen has one head, one bill, one visible eye, one tail, two plausibly attached legs, intact grasping feet, and a convincing near-side wing. The far-side wing is naturally hidden by the side-on pose rather than visibly missing or malformed.

The detached wing and head are clearly intentional supplementary studies. The wing has coherent feather layering and a Cape May Warbler-like white patch, while the head study independently preserves the dark eye, yellow facial frame, chestnut cheek, and plausible bill geometry.

Every visible identification line matches the proposed profile in spelling and meaning: “Small, delicate warbler with a short tail”; “Slender, dark, slightly downcurved bill and dark eye”; “Yellow underparts marked with narrow dark ‘tiger’ streaks”; the adult-male and female/immature cheek description; the olive-upperparts and white-patch/wingbars description; and the dark-legs and white-undertail-coverts description.

The names “Cape May Warbler,” “Setophaga tigrina,” and “Parulidae” are correct. eBird independently confirms the scientific name, family, small size, very slightly downcurved bill, yellow-and-black-streaked adult-male underparts, orange/chestnut cheek, and white wing patch.

The printed measurements—length 4.7–5.1 in (12–13 cm), weight 0.4–0.5 oz (10.2–15.2 g), and wingspan 7.9–8.7 in (20–22 cm)—exactly match the All About Birds measurement table. The repeated BODY LENGTH value is identical and not contradictory.

The wingspan diagram is internally consistent: its 7.9 in (20 cm) minimum is at the bottom, its 8.7 in (22 cm) maximum is at the top, and the values therefore increase upward. Interior ticks are unlabeled subdivisions. “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE” makes clear that the printed specimen is not a life-size scale representation.

Audubon publishes a separately rounded, broader measurement summary, but this does not invalidate the plate because the plate exactly reproduces the direct All About Birds values rather than combining incompatible endpoints.
No map, coordinates, ZIP code, observation site, or local-observation detail appears. “Cape May” occurs only as part of the species’ official common name.
